perspective:
From Harold Padilla’s perspective, the information available to him is:

- I am a project manager. I felt frustrated and anxious because my project team seemed unmotivated, and it was affecting our progress.
- I arranged to meet my friend Arthur, a police officer, at a coffee shop to ask for advice. I told him I needed advice and was at my wit’s end.
- I heard Arthur suggest that I understand what drives each team member individually and have one-on-one conversations with them. I said I would try it and felt more hopeful and relieved.
- I told my team we would have quick one-on-one chats to understand what motivates each of them. Team members said they were open to it or thought it could help. I scheduled time with each of them and asked us to make the project a success together.
- Later, I noticed the team still was not responding well. I felt disappointed and worried about the project’s future.
- I told Arthur that I tried his suggestions but the team still wasn’t responding well. Arthur told me there might be deeper issues, such as personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors, and that I might need to dig deeper. I decided to set up more meetings.
- In those meetings, Team Member 1 told me there was tension between a few people and it was affecting work. Team Member 2 told me they felt overwhelmed by the workload and stressed. I said I would look into resolving conflicts and see about redistributing tasks, and that their well-being is important to me.
- I then told the team we would have regular feedback sessions and team-building activities to create a more supportive environment. Team Member 1 said that sounded great and would help. Team Member 2 agreed and said it was good that concerns were being addressed. I said their input and well-being are crucial to our success.
- I do not have access to Arthur’s private thoughts, the team members’ unspoken concerns, or narrator-only information such as personality types, education, or hidden motives unless it was stated or observed above.
